items.title: Only 1.5 percent of human DNA codes for proteins
items.claim: The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs. Of these, only about 1.5 percent — 45 million bases — encode proteins. The rest was once called 'junk DNA'. Most of it isn't.
items.prompt: What does the non-coding majority actually do?

options.text: It's all junk left over from evolution

It includes promoters, enhancers, insulators, microRNA genes, long non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNA, structural sequences, transposable elements (some still active), and regions whose function is still being mapped
It codes for proteins we haven't found
It's only present in cells that have stopped dividing

items.reveal_title: ENCODE and the redefinition of junk
items.reveal:
The ENCODE Project (2012) reported biochemical activity (transcription, transcription-factor binding, chromatin features) in about 80 percent of the genome. Whether all of this counts as 'function' was hotly debated.

Certain categories of non-coding DNA have clear roles:
- Promoters/enhancers: regulate gene expression in time and place. Disrupting them causes disease (e.g., enhancer mutations causing limb deformity).
- microRNAs: ~22-nucleotide RNAs that tune protein levels.
- Long non-coding RNAs: XIST silences a whole X chromosome in females.
- Transposable elements: about 45 percent of the genome; some still mobile.

Much DNA may also be 'spacer' or accumulated parasitic sequence with no current function — but the cell is full of layers of regulation built from non-coding DNA.
items.why: Genome size was thought to scale with organism complexity. Onions have 5 times more DNA than humans. Most DNA isn't there to encode proteins — and may be doing many things at once.

items.title: Cells make energy by pumping ACID uphill
items.claim: Mitochondria spend most of their energy budget pumping protons across the inner membrane against a steep electrochemical gradient. Only after building this acidic outer space do they let the protons flow back through ATP synthase, capturing the energy.
items.prompt: Why not just make ATP directly during electron transport?

options.text: Chemiosmosis lets the cell decouple ENERGY EXTRACTION (electron transport) from ENERGY USE (ATP synthesis); the proton gradient is a rechargeable battery that links any electron donor to any ATP demand
The gradient is a side-effect with no function

items.reveal_title: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis — initially dismissed, then Nobel-winning
items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that ATP synthesis was driven by a proton gradient, not by direct chemistry. Biochemists hated the idea — it seemed to require a 'metabolic battery' instead of a chemical intermediate. Mitchell was right, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to protons. Electrons flowing through the respiratory chain pump protons OUT, building a pH gradient (~ 0.7 units) and an electric potential (~ 150 mV) — together about 200 mV of proton motive force.

ATP synthase is essentially a rotary motor turned by proton flow. The number of protons per ATP is fractional (about 3.7 to 4) because synthase geometry doesn't match the chemistry of ATP cleanly.
items.why: Energy currency feels like chemistry. Living cells use a physical gradient — a battery — as the actual unit of energy transfer.

items.title: Bacteria count themselves before acting
items.claim: A single Vibrio fischeri bacterium doesn't glow. A dense colony of them lights up the inside of squid light organs and certain Hawaiian fish. The bacteria sense how many bacteria are around them and only switch on bioluminescence when there are enough to matter.
items.prompt: How does a bacterium know how many others are nearby?

options.text: Quorum sensing — each cell secretes a small molecule (an autoinducer); local concentration of autoinducer rises with population density, and at threshold activates gene expression
They wait a fixed time before turning on

items.reveal:
Quorum sensing was discovered in Vibrio fischeri by Hastings and Nealson in the 1970s. Each bacterium continuously produces and secretes a homoserine lactone. At low cell density it diffuses away; at high density it accumulates, enters cells and binds a transcription factor that activates luciferase genes.

Bonnie Bassler's group showed in the 1990s that many bacteria use multiple quorum signals — one species-specific, one universal (AI-2). The universal one allows cross-species 'eavesdropping' on population density of other bacteria.

Pathogens use quorum sensing to time virulence factor expression: stay quiet until there are enough cells to overwhelm the host. Anti-quorum-sensing drugs are an active research area for antibiotic alternatives.
items.why: Bacteria are imagined as solitary cells acting independently. Many of their key behaviours — virulence, biofilm formation, bioluminescence — are coordinated through chemical signalling networks.
